questions.q: What is the ultimate objective of e-logistics?
o: To deliver the right products in the right quantities at the right place and time to the right customer
To replace all warehouses with websites
To remove the need for transportation
To sell more products at a higher price
questions.d: The ultimate objective of e-logistics is to deliver the right products in the right quantities at the right place and time to the right customer.

questions.q: E-logistics is the use of web-based technologies to support which processes?
questions.d: E-logistics uses web-based technologies to support material acquisition, warehousing and transportation, and lets distribution couple routing optimisation with inventory-tracking information.

questions.q: Which example of e-logistics is given on the slides?
o: Internet-based freight auctions that enable spot buying of trucking capacity
questions.d: For example, Internet-based freight auctions enable spot buying of trucking capacity.

questions.q: What does ASN stand for in e-logistics technology?
questions.d: E-logistics technologies include EDI among carriers, shippers and customers, barcoding and scanning, advance ship notices (ASNs), tracking systems, GPS and GIS, the Internet, ERP and more.

questions.q: Electronic data interchange (EDI) on the slides is exchanged among:
questions.d: One listed e-logistics technology is electronic data interchange (EDI) among carriers, shippers and customers.

questions.q: What sets RFID apart according to the slides?
o: It does not need a direct line of sight to read a tag, and tag information can be updated
It must be scanned in direct line of sight
Its tags can never be changed
It only works for whole pallets, not individual units
questions.d: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tracks individual units of goods, does not require a direct line of sight to read a tag, and the information on the tag is updatable.

questions.q: E-procurement supports which key procurement processes?
o: Requisitioning, sourcing, contracting, ordering and payment
questions.d: E-procurement uses web-based technology to support requisitioning, sourcing, contracting, ordering and payment, using online catalogues, contracts, purchase orders and shipping notices.

questions.q: Reducing paper-driven transactions through e-procurement is linked to what drop in net greenhouse gas production (Romm, 2000)?
questions.d: Savings from e-procurement: ideally reducing all paper-driven transactions, linked to a 25% drop in net greenhouse gas production (Romm, 2000).

questions.q: How does e-logistics support 'postponement' in inventory and warehousing?
o: Fast information means less inventory is needed (JIT)
Products are stored longer before sale
Orders are delayed until the end of the year
Warehouses are moved next to every customer
questions.d: Postponement: less inventory because of the quick speed of information (JIT). Warehousing can also be aggregated and centralised, so it does not need to be next to the customer.

questions.q: Substituting durable goods with information improves efficiency and reduces:
questions.d: Information integration, substituting durable goods with information, gives better efficiency and less bullwhip effect.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the B2C e-logistics processes on the slides?
questions.d: The seven B2C e-logistics processes: method of payment, check product availability, arrange shipments, insurance, replenishment, contact with customers, and returns.

questions.q: Which B2C process is described as the biggest activity (labour, energy, money) in e-logistics?
questions.d: Arranging shipments: electronic shipping is quick, while physical products need the best shipping method for the service level. It is the biggest activity in labour, energy and money.

questions.q: In B2C payments, cash on delivery (COD) is paid:
questions.d: Payment can be made at the time of order (e-payment such as PayPal, or credit card) or at the time of delivery (COD).

questions.q: In replenishment, shipping materials, scanners, totes and carts count as:
questions.d: Replenishment examines all physical inventory and reorders as needed: product (on shelves or material to make it) and non-product (shipping materials, machine parts, scanners, totes, carts).

questions.q: Why should e-logistics keep customers informed with order, payment, shipping and tracking messages?
o: Because back-door operations are invisible to the customer
Because customers must approve each warehouse task
Because the law requires a phone call for every order
Because it removes the need for insurance
questions.d: With an invisible process (back-door operations), the customer needs to be informed as much as possible: order confirmation, payment success, shipping confirmation, tracking and any problems.

questions.q: Which of these is a listed challenge of e-logistics?
o: There are too few online stores
questions.d: Challenges: higher e-commerce return rates, a culture focused on sales not returns, unknown return volumes, lack of retailing experience, and many sources of returns. Responses include subcontracted return stores and third-party reverse logistics providers.

questions.q: For electronic payments, payment should be verified before the product is shipped.
questions.d: For electronic payments, a system of verification of payment is needed before shipping.

questions.q: Internet technologies have only helped large corporations compete for market share.
questions.d: E-business technologies, particularly the Internet, let organisations of all sizes connect with partners and compete for market share, which before was only possible for large corporations.

questions.q: Transportation costs may increase because of centralised warehousing.
questions.d: Centralising warehousing means less waste and energy for extra locations, but transportation costs may increase.

questions.q: If a product is out of stock, the customer should not be told until it ships.
questions.d: If possible, inform the customer about availability before the order is placed. If the product is out of stock or will take time to make, inform the customer of the delay.
